title: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors

fields.label: Label
fields.value: 2D cellular automata can produce complex overall shapes, not just complex interiors

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: A simple 2D cellular automaton (a cell turns black when exactly three of its eight neighbors are black, otherwise unchanged) can grow patterns whose overall shapes keep changing with no simple form, so complexity can appear in a pattern's overall shape as well as in its interior.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: there can be great complexity not only in the detailed arrangement of black and white cells in a two-dimensional cellular automaton pattern, but also in the overall shape of the pattern.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 5, “Two Dimensions and Beyond”; section “Cellular Automata” (from p. 170), p. 176. Scope: two-dimensional growth-type cellular automata

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch05-04: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.88

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The rule is exact, inexpensive to run, and the distinction between boundary and interior can be measured directly. Existing computation can confirm complex finite boundary dynamics, which is sufficient for the existential core.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Reproduce the exactly specified growth rule, track boundary shape descriptors over time, and compare predictability, periodicity, symmetry, and compressibility against simple-shape growth controls. Persistent irregular boundary dynamics confirms that complexity occurs in overall shape.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Finite runs do not exclude eventual regularity.

No simple form is relative to the chosen shape descriptors.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.92
data adequacy: 0.82
discriminating power: 0.87
analysis feasibility: 0.94
operationalizability: 0.86

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The rule and the seed are fixed, and the claim is that this simple growth rule produces overall shapes that keep changing, not only complicated interiors. That is a finite, exact simulation with a shape statistic that either keeps evolving or locks onto a simple form. A long confirming run settles the existence claim as stated; only a stronger 'forever' reading would remain open.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Evolve the rule 'turn black if exactly three of eight neighbors are black, otherwise stay the same' from a row of eleven black cells, and track the outline's Fourier spectrum and diameter over many thousands of steps. Continued change of the outline without collapse to a fixed shape confirms complexity of the overall form; stabilization to a simple growing shape would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
A shape that keeps changing for thousands of steps can still settle later, so the run bounds the claim rather than proving it for all time.

Interior complexity can be mistaken for complexity of the outline unless the outline is measured separately.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.7
data adequacy: 0.8
analysis feasibility: 0.85
data existence: 0.9
operationalizability: 0.8

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: The 8-neighbour outer-totalistic 2D cellular automaton 'a cell becomes black when exactly three of its eight neighbours are black, otherwise it is unchanged' (NKS code 174826, Life-like notation B3/S012345678), started from a row of eleven black cells, keeps growing for 1000 steps while the normalised outline of the whole pattern keeps changing on the scale of the pattern itself and never settles to a simple geometric form (circle, square, diamond or octagon), whereas simple growth rules settle to a fixed simple outline.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py evolves NKS code 174826 (B3/S012345678) from a row of 11 black cells for 1000 steps on a dynamically padded numpy grid, and at 8 checkpoints records population, mean radius, convex-hull solidity and the normalised outer-radius profile rho_t(theta) in 360 angular bins about the pattern centroid. It computes D(t1,t2) = mean |rho_t1 - rho_t2| between checkpoints and the distance from rho_1000 to five reference profiles (circle, two squares, two octagons). The same pipeline is run on two simple-growth controls (8-neighbour and 4-neighbour 'black if any neighbour black') and on code 175850 from a row of 7 for comparison. Runtime about 20 s.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Run the rule for T = 1000 steps from a row of 11 black cells. Let rho_t(theta) be the outer radius of the occupied set from the pattern centroid in 360 angular bins, normalised by its mean, and D(t1,t2) the mean absolute difference between rho_t1 and rho_t2. PASS (supports) if all three hold: (a) growth continues: mean radius R(1000) >= 1.5 * R(500) and the population is larger at step 1000 than at step 500; (b) the outline keeps changing: D(500,1000) >= 0.05 and D(750,1000) >= 0.03, while both control rules (8-neighbour 'black if any neighbour black', which grows a square, and 4-neighbour 'black if any neighbour black', which grows a diamond) give D(500,1000) <= 0.02; (c) the outline at step 1000 is not a simple form: the minimum over the reference family {circle, axis-aligned square, 45-degree square, regular octagon at 0 and 22.5 degrees} of the mean absolute difference between rho_1000 and the reference profile is >= 0.05, while for each control rule the same minimum is <= 0.03.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. FAIL (refutes) if growth stops (population unchanged over steps 900-1000) or if the outline converges to a simple form: D(500,1000) < 0.02 and the minimum simple-shape distance at step 1000 is < 0.03. Any other combination is 'mixed' (e.g. shape still changing but growth slowing, or controls not behaving as expected, which would mean the descriptor is not discriminating).

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: exact deterministic computation; descriptor resolution 1 degree

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: Wolfram's claim (pp. 176, 181) is existential: this one rule from this one seed produces an overall shape that 'seems continually to go on changing, with no simple overall form'. 'Overall shape' is mapped to the normalised angular outer-radius profile of the occupied set, so interior texture is ignored; 'no simple form' is mapped to distance from a small pre-declared family of simple convex shapes and to non-convergence of the outline between steps 500, 750 and 1000. 'Continually' can only be bounded by the run length; a finite run cannot exclude eventual regularity. Code 175850 (the '3 or 5 of 8' rule from p. 177, row of 7), which the book says is rough on small scales but smooth on large scales, is run as an additional comparison but is not part of the criterion.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Enumerated evolution of the 2D outer-totalistic 8-neighbour cellular automaton, NKS code 174826 (birth on exactly 3 black neighbours, otherwise unchanged), generated by analysis.py

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
A 1000-step run bounds 'continually' but cannot exclude eventual regularity of the outline; growth was still linear (mean radius 128 -> 251 cells between steps 500 and 1000, about 0.25 cells per step) and the outline change between checkpoints showed no downward trend (0.08-0.39).

'Simple form' was operationalised as a pre-declared family of five convex shapes plus convergence of the outline; a shape could in principle be 'simple' in a sense not covered (e.g. a fixed irregular polygon), but the outline also failed to converge (D(750,1000) = 0.16), which no fixed limiting shape allows.

The outline descriptor is the outer radius per angular bin, so interior holes (solidity 0.49 of the convex hull) are ignored, as the claim requires.

The comparison rule code 175850 behaves as the book describes (D(500,1000) = 0.0066, closest to a circle at distance 0.025), which supports the discriminating power of the descriptor but is not part of the criterion.
